Rules:

# Liberal Democrats Manifesto 2015 Summary

## Core Vision

The Liberal Democrats present themselves as advocates for a "stronger economy and fairer society," positioning themselves between Conservative-only spending cuts and Labour approaches. They emphasize their five years of Coalition government as validation of their governing capability, promising to build on achievements like raising the personal tax allowance and protecting the NHS budget.

## Economic Policy

The party commits to balancing the budget by 2017/18 through a "fair" mix of spending cuts and targeted tax increases on the wealthy, banks, and polluters. They reject Conservative proposals for cuts-only deficit reduction, arguing this would damage public services. Key economic priorities include supporting advanced manufacturing, creating a British Business Bank, expanding the Green Investment Bank, and investing in renewable energy infrastructure to create a "high-skill, low-carbon economy."

## Taxation

The flagship tax pledge is raising the Personal Allowance to £12,500, delivering approximately £400 in additional tax cuts for working people. They propose a High Value Property Levy on homes worth over £2 million, tougher action on corporate tax avoidance, and restrictions on non-domiciled status.

## Public Services

The manifesto promises £8 billion additional investment in the NHS by 2020 and £500 million annually for mental health services, establishing waiting time standards for mental health treatment equivalent to physical health care. On education, they guarantee funding from early years through age 19, promise qualified teachers in every classroom, and aim to eliminate child illiteracy by 2025.

## Environment

Environmental commitments include five "Green Laws" covering nature protection, resource efficiency, green transport, zero-carbon Britain by 2050, and green buildings. They pledge to achieve 60% renewable electricity by 2030 and create National Nature Parks.

## Constitutional Reform

The party advocates for completing Scottish devolution through the Smith Commission, devolving further powers to Wales, maintaining EU membership, introducing proportional representation and votes at 16, and establishing a UK Constitutional Convention to produce a written constitution. They remain committed to reforming the House of Lords into an elected chamber.
